q: Dennett's thesis is that belief is objective, yet discernible only from a certain predictive strategy. That makes him (apparently) both:
w: A dualist and a behaviorist
An eliminativist and a functionalist
An identity theorist and a dualist
e: Realism likens belief to a virus (objective). Interpretationism likens it to having style (relative). Dennett says the choice is a false dichotomy.

q: The 'physical stance' predicts behavior by using:
a: Its physical makeup and the laws of physics
w: What it was designed to do
The beliefs and desires it ought to have
Its past behavior in similar situations
e: The system's physical constitution plus the laws of physics. Laplace's grand but impractical strategy, though a cook uses a local version to predict a pot boiling over.

q: Predicting an alarm clock will ring when set, without knowing if it's spring-wound or battery-driven, uses the:
w: Physical stance
Intentional stance
Astrological stance
e: You assume it's designed to behave a certain way. But to predict it pumped full of liquid helium, revert to the physical stance.

q: The intentional stance treats an object as a rational agent and attributes:
a: The beliefs and desires it ought to have
w: Whatever beliefs it reports having
Only the beliefs that happen to be true
Random beliefs, kept if they predict well
e: The beliefs and desires it OUGHT to have given its place in the world and purpose. Then you predict it will act to further its goals in light of its beliefs.

q: What's Dennett's basic rule for attributing beliefs?
a: All relevant truths its experience made available
w: Every truth that it could possibly come to know
Only the beliefs it states out loud when asked
Only the beliefs its designer intended it to have
e: Attribute all truths relevant to the system's interests that its experience has made available. This leads to the implication that true believers mainly believe truths. False beliefs need a special genealogy grown from true ones.

q: The baked beans example ('How many?') illustrates that language:
a: Pushes us into more specific desires than we had
w: Has nothing to do with what we actually desire
Captures our desires exactly as they already are
Is irrelevant to what we believe or want
e: Forces us to commit to desires more specific than we antecedently had. Focusing on these effects while ignoring their distortion misleads us into thinking beliefs are sentences stored in the head.

q: How rational do we assume an intentional system is, initially?
a: Perfectly rational, revised down as needed
w: Not rational at all until proven otherwise
As rational as an average human
Rational only about simple matters
e: Perfectly rational, then revise downward as circumstances dictate. We only need it to be rational enough to reach the implications relevant to its current predicament.

q: Which does Dennett NOT use as an example of the intentional strategy working?
w: A clam
Apple trees
Lightning
e: A lectern, which he uses as a case that should be disqualified. The lectern can be interpreted as 'wanting to stay at the center of civilization', but this adds no predictive power we didn't already have.

q: Dennett says the decision to adopt the intentional stance is free, but:
w: Its results are purely subjective
It only works when applied to humans
It can never fail once it is adopted
e: The facts about its success or failure are perfectly objective. He rejects the radical interpretationist reading where belief depends on the observer's cleverness.

q: In Nozick's objection, Laplacean Martian super-physicists predict our behavior at the microphysical level. Dennett says they'd still miss:
a: Real patterns visible only from the intentional stance
w: The precise physical states of each of our brains
The details of every one of our physical movements
Nothing at all, since they'd already know everything
e: The objective patterns in human behavior visible only from the intentional stance. Indefinitely many finger motions could have placed the same 500-share GM order. That's a real pattern, like the many ways of being a sparkplug.

q: After the call 'bring the boss to dinner... pick up wine', the Earthling's prediction would look to the Martian like:
w: A simple physics calculation
An obvious guess
A random coincidence
e: Magic, as marvelous as the fatalistic 'appointment in Samarra'. Fatalists are wrong but 'almost right'. Intentional patterns impose themselves 'with great vigor', absorbing physical perturbations.

q: In cases like self-deception or contradictory beliefs, Dennett's 'milder realism' says:
a: There may be no fact of the matter
w: They have determinate beliefs we can't detect
Belief attribution is purely subjective
Such people have no beliefs at all
e: There may be no fact of the matter about exactly which beliefs someone has, though that itself is an objective fact. A strong realist would insist on hidden determinate beliefs.

q: As we enrich a thermostat's links to the world (vision, geography, fuel purchasing), what happens to the semantics of its internal states?
a: They grow more specific, toward one interpretation
w: They become poorer and less specific over time
They stay exactly the same no matter what is added
They become impossible to interpret in any way
e: They become richer and more specific until a unique interpretation is practically dictated. There's no magic moment between thermostat and human. The differences are of (enormous) degree.

q: The 'easy' answer to why the intentional strategy works on humans is:
a: Evolution designed us to be rational
w: We have a language of thought
We are conditioned by reinforcement
We have immaterial souls
e: Evolution designed us to be rational: to believe and want what we ought to. True and brief but uninformative. The hard question is how the machinery actually works, and we don't yet know.

q: Dennett says believers in a language of thought often confuse which two empirical claims?
a: That patterns are real, and that brains mirror them
w: That brains exist and that minds exist
That animals think and that computers think
That physics is true and that psychology is true
e: That intentional patterns are real, and that they're produced by an isomorphic pattern in the brain. The first claim is confirmed beyond skepticism. The second is plausible but not inevitable. The argument for it is 'what else could it be?'

q: What problem does Dennett say the brain has somehow solved, motivating language-of-thought theories?
w: The frame problem
The halting problem
The mind-body problem
e: Small increases in inputs explode internal complexity. Some elegant, generative representation system must be responsible.
